variants.name: Typed Express middleware chain
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript adds signatures to the Node runtime rather than a new mechanism: RequestHandler and ErrorRequestHandler type the middleware stack, app.use fixes the order, and the router types the dispatch target's path parameters. What replaces the classic structure: the same middleware array plus router, now checked by the compiler, so a missing next call or a wrongly typed handler fails at build time; decorator frameworks (NestJS, ts.ED) and file-convention entries (Next.js proxy.ts) generate the same chain for you.
pitfalls: RequestHandler and ErrorRequestHandler have different arities: an error handler typed as RequestHandler compiles but is never invoked.

Declaration merging on Express.Request is global, so augmenting the request type in one module advertises those fields to every handler; keep the augmented type honest about what middleware guarantees.
Type assertions on req.params or req.body do not validate runtime input - pair the typed handler with a schema check.

variants.name: Next.js file-convention proxy on the edge runtime
variants.implementation_notes: Next.js expresses the front controller as a file convention: one exported proxy function (the renamed middleware convention) runs before every route matched by config.matcher, can rewrite or redirect or return a response directly, and is deployed to the CDN edge where it cannot share module state with render code. What replaces the classic structure: the file convention replaces the programmatic app object and the matcher replaces the route table, giving one entry point per project instead of one app object.
pitfalls: Without a matcher the proxy runs for static assets too, so authentication redirects can block CSS and JS; and it is not a substitute for authorization inside server functions, which must enforce it as well.
The edge runtime is not Node: no shared globals or module state and no Node APIs, so the proxy must stay stateless per request.
A matcher change or a file move silently removes coverage - treat the matcher as security-critical configuration and verify it in tests.
